feedback: If a learner thinks air is 'nothing', have them blow on their hand: 'You just felt the air push — so air is real stuff, even though we can't see it.'
If a learner thinks wind must come from one place like the sky, show it can be made from any direction by fanning: 'Wind is air moving from place to place, not pouring out of one spot.'
Distinguish gently: 'A fan and your breath are moving air YOU make; outdoor wind is moving air outdoors — same idea, different source.'
activities.intendedInsight: Air is real stuff you can feel, and wind is simply air that is moving. You can make moving air yourself with your breath or a fan — the same idea as outdoor wind, just a different source.
learnerActions: Blow on the back of your own hand and feel the push.
Wave a hand or a fan at your face and feel the moving air.
Wave a streamer or strip of paper and watch it flutter in the air you move.
Talk about where outdoor wind is the same idea (moving air) but comes from outside rather than from you.
Indoors with the windows shut, work out how you could still make a little wind yourself (blow, fan, wave) — showing wind is just air moving, not something from a single fixed source.
activities.title: Make your own wind

feedback: Correct answer: 'It's the other way round. Wind is moving air. The moving air pushes the branches, which is why they wave — the trees aren't making the wind. We can't see the air itself, but we can see what it does.'
If a learner names the moving object as the cause, flip it: show a still day (nothing waves), then a fan making a still branch wave — the air moves the object, not the other way round.
Keep the real cause of wind aside: 'We're not working out what makes the wind blow today — just that the wind moves the trees, not the trees making the wind.'
activities.intendedInsight: Wind is moving air, and the moving air pushes the branches, which is why they wave — the trees do not make the wind. Cause goes from moving air to moving object, not the reverse.
learnerActions: Look at or imagine a windy day with tree branches waving about.
Consider a claim: 'The trees are making the wind by waving.' Decide whether it is right and explain why.
Compare a windless day where nothing waves with a fan (moving air) making a still branch wave — notice the moving air moves the branch.
State in your own words what wind actually is and what is really happening with the trees.
activities.title: Which way does the cause go? (trees and wind)

feedback: For sorting, link back to the scene: 'A leaf blows away in a breeze, but it takes a much stronger wind to move heavier things like a hat or branches — and a big heavy rock barely moves at all.'
If ordering is muddled, anchor on effects: 'Fluttering leaves is gentler than a bending tree.'
If a learner says you can SEE the wind, correct: 'We see what the wind does and the things it carries — not the moving air itself.'
activities.intendedInsight: Checking that wind is moving air known by its effects, that some things move in wind and heavy things resist, and that strength runs along a spectrum from breeze to gale.
learnerActions: Sort objects into 'the wind can move this easily' (kite, leaves, flag, hat, washing) versus 'the wind can't easily move this' (heavy rock).
Put effects in order from gentle to strong: leaves flutter → branches sway → hard to walk / tree bends.
Answer 'what is wind?' and explain how you know it's windy if you can't see the wind.
Tell a gentle breeze apart from a strong gale and give an example of each.
activities.title: Sort and order by what wind does

feedback: Prompt for a second clue if a learner gives only one: 'That's one way — the flag is flapping. What else tells you it's windy?'
Praise effect-based answers: 'Yes — you feel it push and you see things move; both tell you the air is moving.'
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating that we detect wind only by its effects, and that strength varies, strengthens the observe-by-effects reasoning.
learnerActions: Answer a prompt such as 'How do you KNOW it's windy if you can't see the wind? Give me two ways.'
Describe the difference between a gentle breeze and a strong gale in your own words.
Work out, with windows shut indoors, how you could make a little wind yourself.
activities.title: How do you know it's windy? (talking it through)
